thread.title: Stock Price Goes Down, Dividend Yield Available Goes Up. Yes, It's That Simple - TransCanada Corporation (NYSE:TRP)

author: Dale Roberts
title: Stock Price Goes Down, Dividend Yield Available Goes Up. Yes, It's That Simple - TransCanada Corporation (NYSE:TRP)
text:
It has not been pretty for those who watch stock prices of some higher yielders. Here's a chart showing a popular ETF that covers the Canadian High Dividend Yield space. Courtesy of portfoliovisualizer.com here's the Vanguard VDY on the Toronto Stock Exchange. The time period is January of 2017 to end of May 2018. The chart does not include dividends or dividend reinvestment. As always past performance does not guarantee future returns.
That does not look too bad. Of course no one is going to get rich off of 3.5% annual returns, but it's better than sitting on the sidelines. That said, I conduct more of a wide moat index skimming venture for the Canadian holdings in my personal RSP (Retirement) account. I hold my Canadian Wide Moat 7 and I've experienced the concentration risks. While I have confidence in the long term dividends and financial health of my Wide Moat 7, it is obviously exposed to that risk. If even 2, 3, or 4 get hit hard the whole Canadian portfolio component is going to take a great hit. Here's my Wide Moat 7 for the same period. Once again my Wide Moat 7 consists of the three biggest banks in Canada by way of Royal Bank of Canada ( RY ), Toronto Dominion Bank ( TD ), Scotiabank ( BNS ), two of the largest telcos in Bell Canada ( BCE ) and Telus ( TU ) plus the largest pipeline operators in Enbridge ( ENB ) and TransCanada ( TRP ).
OK, so that's not as bad as I thought, and once again it's surprising how few companies it can take to track an index. For the record, I would not suggest using only 7 companies in the attempt to track or skim an index, I'd go for 8, just kidding :) You may decide to go for 20 companies or more.
All said, within my Wide Moat 7 there was some incredible disruption. Here are the individual holdings for the period.
The banks.
Nope, those are the winners. Thanks goodness for 'diversification'.
The Telco's.
Nope that's not the trouble. Put those two Telco's together in portfolio form and they outperform the Vanguard ETF by .5% annual. Though Bell has certainly had its price issues.
So here's trouble, the pipelines.
Those pipelines have been beat up read bad, and Enbridge to the greater degree. ENB is down some 27% and that's with dividend reinvestment. The price has declined by over 30%. But with each drop in share price, up goes the dividend yield available. It's simple math of course. The reason for the bigger dividend payments being available is due to the simple fact that a lower share price allows you to buy more shares. And certainly that higher share count will also become a benefit if or when one decides to sell shares, you have more shares available to sell to generate profits. One has greater dividends payments and greater potential total returns. Now of course, the investor would need the dividend to remain stable (or hopefully growing) and we'd also need that share price to recover over time moving to positive territory based on your average share price paid.
As you've likely guessed, I took advantage of those lower prices and bigger dividends over the last year. As my readers will know I recently Said Goodbye To My Regular Pay Cheque and moved to full time writing and blogging. Approaching that semi retirement date I beefed up on Enbridge and TransCanada. I was able to obtain dividend yields of up to 6.5% on Enbridge and 5.5% on TransCanada. Even though I certainly know that stocks are not bonds (no matter how big one might think the moat), I reallocated some bond proceeds to Bell and Telus. That selling of some bonds and moving to the Telco bond substitutes was enabled as my RSP account group plan monies from Tangerine are now available to move from that group plan to my self directed discount brokerage retirement account. Those monies soon to be in cash will soon be on their way to my self directed account. They will remain a cash component with some of the proceeds moving to my new bond allocation. You can have a look at what I did with my stinky bonds in this article .
Here's the simply math on dividend yields available, and yes I know it is not news to all, but perhaps a useful to reminder to those who might overthink things a bit.
Here's a year to date chart for TransCanada on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
If the indicated dividend rate had been constant at $2.76 over the last few months, and with a current share price of 53.98 that gives us a current yield offering of 5.11%. That's 2.76 dividend by 53.87 x 100. If we go back one year to June of 2017 the share price as in the area of $64. The yield available would be 4.3%. Investors who had the fortitude to buy when the company and sector was out of market favour were rewarded with a dividend that's almost 20% greater. How's that for dividend growth? Now of course over the last year things are even better as TransCanada increased its dividend in January or 2018. Here's the recent dividend growth history from the TransCanada investor page.
Heading into my semi retirement phase, and making my last few investments before I start harvesting dividends and bond income and selling shares to create income, I was offered what might turn out to be a wonderful opportunity. I was able to greatly boost my share counts and those future dividend payments. Of course I am also hoping for continued dividend growth. There was a lot of chatter on Seeking Alpha boards about Enbridge and TransCanada and Kinder Morgan ( KMI ) and other pipeline players. I read with interested but ignored all and trusted the two Canadian pipeline companies that have treated me well for over a decade. Well let's say I trusted management and their mission and business plan.
I also trusted Bell as it was down in price adding to that bond 'proxy'. I know tsk tsk. That will be my greatest dividend payment moving forward, followed by Telus and then Enbridge. In fact Day 1 of 'retirement' offered a nice surprise as Enbridge paid that juicy dividend. As I wrote in Day 1 Of Retirement And The Dividends Arrive As A Sign From Above , I made more on my first day of not working, compared to the day before when I was at my full time job.
When we have an investment that pays a generous dividend, and the investment value will be mostly gained or accessed by those dividend payments compared to dividends and share harvesting, perhaps it's best to keep it simple and keep the eye on the dividend. Many investors seem to mangle their investment metaphors mixing income investing with value investing and other factors. What will be important is the dividend payments and the dividend health which certainly comes back to company health and management vision and execution.
I am happy to have trusted buy and hold and add; happy to have trusted the companies that I own. Only time will tell.
Happy Investing.
